# Generating an installation access token for a GitHub App
## [Generating an installation access token](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/authenticating-with-a-github-app/generating-an-installation-access-token-for-a-github-app#generating-an-installation-access-token)
```shell
curl --request POST \
   --url "https://api.github.com/app/installations/INSTALLATION_ID/access_tokens" \
   --header "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" \
   --header "Authorization: Bearer JWT" \
   --header "X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2026-03-10"
```

The installation access token will expire after 1 hour.

# Generating an installation access token for a GitHub App

Learn how to generate an installation access token for your GitHub App.

Copy as Markdown

## In this article

## [About installation access tokens](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/authenticating-with-a-github-app/generating-an-installation-access-token-for-a-github-app\#about-installation-access-tokens)

In order to authenticate as an app installation, you must generate an installation access token. For more information about authenticating as an app installation, see [Authenticating as a GitHub App installation](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/authenticating-with-a-github-app/authenticating-as-a-github-app-installation).

Note

Instead of generating an installation access token, you can use GitHub's Octokit SDKs to authenticate as an app. The SDK will take care of generating an installation access token for you and will regenerate the token once it expires. For more information about authenticating as an app installation, see [Authenticating as a GitHub App installation](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/authenticating-with-a-github-app/authenticating-as-a-github-app-installation).

You should keep your installation access token secure. For more information, see [Best practices for creating a GitHub App](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/about-creating-github-apps/best-practices-for-creating-a-github-app).

Note

Starting April 27, 2026, GitHub began a staged rollout of a stateless format (`ghs_APPID_JWT`) to all newly minted GitHub App installation tokens, making them more performant and improving the reliability of our API surface. If your application expects or relies on installation tokens being exactly 40 characters long, it may not handle this new token format correctly. You can now validate your apps and workflows using a temporary request header that lets you enable the token format on demand. For more information about the temporary header, see [the GitHub blog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-05-15-github-app-installation-tokens-per-request-override-header).

## [Generating an installation access token](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/authenticating-with-a-github-app/generating-an-installation-access-token-for-a-github-app\#generating-an-installation-access-token)

1. Generate a JSON web token (JWT) for your app. For more information, see [Generating a JSON Web Token (JWT) for a GitHub App](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/authenticating-with-a-github-app/generating-a-json-web-token-jwt-for-a-github-app).

2. Get the ID of the installation that you want to authenticate as.

If you are responding to a webhook event, the webhook payload will include the installation ID.

You can also use the REST API to find the ID for an installation of your app. For example, you can get an installation ID with the `GET /users/{username}/installation`, `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/installation`, `GET /orgs/{org}/installation`, or `GET /app/installations` endpoints. For more information, see [REST API endpoints for GitHub Apps](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/apps/apps).

You can also find the app ID on the settings page for your app. The app ID is different from the client ID. For more information about navigating to the settings page for your GitHub App, see [Modifying a GitHub App registration](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/maintaining-github-apps/modifying-a-github-app-registration#navigating-to-your-github-app-settings).

3. Send a REST API `POST` request to `/app/installations/INSTALLATION_ID/access_tokens`. Include your JSON web token in the `Authorization` header of your request. Replace `INSTALLATION_ID` with the ID of the installation that you want to authenticate as.

For example, send this curl request. Replace `INSTALLATION_ID` with the ID of the installation and `JWT` with your JSON web token:


```shell
curl --request POST \
   --url "https://api.github.com/app/installations/INSTALLATION_ID/access_tokens" \
   --header "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" \
   --header "Authorization: Bearer JWT" \
   --header "X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2026-03-10"
```


Optionally, you can use the `repositories` or `repository_ids` body parameters to specify individual repositories that the installation access token can access. If you don't use `repositories` or `repository_ids` to grant access to specific repositories, the installation access token will have access to all repositories that the installation was granted access to. The installation access token cannot be granted access to repositories that the installation was not granted access to. You can list up to 500 repositories.

Optionally, use the `permissions` body parameter to specify the permissions that the installation access token should have. If `permissions` is not specified, the installation access token will have all of the permissions that were granted to the app. The installation access token cannot be granted permissions that the app was not granted.

The response will include an installation access token, the time that the token expires, the permissions that the token has, and the repositories that the token can access, if applicable. The installation access token will expire after 1 hour.

For more information about this endpoint, see [REST API endpoints for GitHub Apps](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/apps/apps).



Note




In most cases, you can use `Authorization: Bearer` or `Authorization: token` to pass a token. However, if you are passing a JSON web token (JWT), you must use `Authorization: Bearer`.

### Body
Hello all,
I have created my public github app for clients to use and I have set up everything (from fetching code from GitHub to getting access token) using [this](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/authenticating-with-a-github-app/generating-a-user-access-token-for-a-github-app) documentation.
The only problem I am facing is that the default expiration of the github app token is 28800 seconds (which is 8 hours). I understand that there is a refresh token which I receive along with token with which I can automate the process of refreshing the token before 8 hours. But isn't there a convenient process by which I can simply set a longer expiry duration at the time of generating the token?
Edit: It would be great if there is a parameter by which we can mention a desirable expiration date instead of default 8 hours fixed by github.

## Description

[![@Afoucaul](https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/10498784?u=df6ddbd285eeee1e5749dcfe0bf6560ecfff478a&v=4&size=48)](https://github.com/Afoucaul)

opened [on Mar 29, 2024on Mar 29, 2024](https://github.com/actions/create-github-app-token/issues/121#issue-2215120385)

Issue body actions

I'm running a workflow (`target-workflow.yml`) in another repository (`target-repo`) of my organization using [https://github.com/aurelien-baudet/workflow-dispatch](https://github.com/aurelien-baudet/workflow-dispatch) (v2).

To that end I'm generating an app token with `actions/create-github-app-token@v1`.

I can generate the token with no issues, and `aurelien-baudet/workflow-dispatch@v2` manages to trigger `target-workflow.yml` all right as well.

However, after some time, fetching the status of `target-workflow` starts to fail with `Warning: Failed to get workflow status: Bad credentials`. This causes my parent job to fail.

That seems to start happening after exactly 1h.

Am I correct that the token expires after 1h? Is it documented somewhere?

Also, is there a way to extend the lifetime of this token? Otherwise, do you suggest a workaround?

My workflow:

```
name: Run target-workflow.yml in other target-repo

permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read

jobs:
  run-target-workflow:
    name: Run target-workflow
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/create-github-app-token@v1
        id: app-token
        with:
          app-id: ...  # My app id
          private-key: ...  # My private key
          repositories: "target-repo"

      - name: Run workflow in target-repo
        uses: aurelien-baudet/workflow-dispatch@v2
        with:
          ref: main
          repo: target-repo
          workflow: target-workflow.yml
          wait-for-completion: true
          wait-for-completion-timeout: 2h
          token: ${{ steps.app-token.outputs.token }}
          inputs: ...  # The relevant inputs to target-workflow
```

The output of `aurelien-baudet/workflow-dispatch@v2` step:

```
Run aurelien-baudet/workflow-dispatch@v2
Workflow triggered 🚀
You can follow the running workflow here: https://github.com/...
Warning: The `set-output` command is deprecated and will be disabled soon. Please upgrade to using Environment Files. For more information see: https://github.blog/changelog/2022-10-11-github-actions-deprecating-save-state-and-set-output-commands/
Waiting for workflow completion
Warning: Failed to get workflow status: Bad credentials
Warning: Failed to get workflow status: Bad credentials
Warning: Failed to get workflow status: Bad credentials
...
```

> That seems to start happening after exactly 1h.

That is by design. Installation access tokens expire after 1h, there is no way to extend it, I'm afraid. We should probably document that in the README for folks who don't know. We could even log out a message for folks to see when they investigate problems. We could also export the expiration time as an additional output 🤔

More actions

For long-running processes, I usually write my actions to accept the app ID and private key. If you build your action in JS/TS, you can use the `App` constructor which provides lots of helpful APIs: [https://github.com/octokit/octokit.js?tab=readme-ov-file#app-client](https://github.com/octokit/octokit.js?tab=readme-ov-file#app-client). If you use the `app.getInstallationOctokit(installationId)` API, the returned `octokit` instance will auto-renew the installation access token.

If you want something lower-level, you can use `@octokit/auth-app`: [https://github.com/octokit/auth-app.js?tab=readme-ov-file#authenticate-as-installation](https://github.com/octokit/auth-app.js?tab=readme-ov-file#authenticate-as-installation). When you [use the authentication strategy with an `Octokit` constructor](https://github.com/octokit/auth-app.js?tab=readme-ov-file#usage-with-octokit), it will auto-renew the installation access token as well.

Question
### 💬 Feature/Topic Area
API
### Body
Our code currently uses:
POST /app/installations/{installation\_id}/access\_tokens
to generate installation access tokens for customer organizations.
We understand that API rate limits for installation tokens are isolated per installation, which scales well across multiple organizations.
However, I would like clarification specifically around the scalability and throttling characteristics of the installation token generation endpoint itself.
Does the endpoint:
POST /app/installations/{installation\_id}/access\_tokens
fall under:
i) app-level throttling,
ii) installation-level throttling,
iii) secondary rate limits/abuse protection,
iv) or a separate internal quota model?
Are token generation requests isolated per installation, or are they effectively shared at the GitHub App level?
In a large multi-tenant deployment (many organizations/installations), is there recommended guidance on:
maximum token generation frequency,
expected scaling behavior,
concurrency considerations,
or token caching best practices?
Our current understanding is:
installation API quotas are isolated per installation,
but installation token creation itself may still be governed by centralized app/authentication throttling and secondary abuse detection.
Will this scale safely for multiple organizations? | 1You must be logged in to vote All reactions ## Replies: 5 comments · 6 replies Comment options ### Uh oh! There was an error while loading. [Please reload this page](https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/196652). # {{title}} Quote reply ### [![](https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/163284973?s=64&v=4)\ ChadwickBroski](https://github.com/ChadwickBroski) [on May 22May 22, 2026](https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/196652\#discussioncomment-17021941) | # GitHub App Installation Token Generation — Scaling & Rate Limit Behavior ## Endpoint ``` POST /app/installations/{installation_id}/access_tokens ``` This endpoint creates a GitHub App installation access token using a GitHub App JWT. Installation access tokens: - expire after 1 hour - are scoped to a specific installation - are used for authenticated API requests on behalf of that installation * * * ## Key Clarification There are **two separate concepts** involved: 1. **Creating installation tokens** 2. **Using installation tokens** These behave differently from a rate-limiting perspective. * * * ## 1\. Installation Token Usage Once an installation access token is created, API requests made with that token use the installation’s own REST API rate limit bucket. GitHub documents installation rate limits as: - minimum: **5,000 requests/hour** - GitHub Enterprise Cloud: **15,000 requests/hour** - may scale up to **12,500 requests/hour** for large orgs based on repositories/users This quota is effectively isolated per installation. * * * ## 2\. Installation Token Creation The token generation endpoint itself: ``` POST /app/installations/{installation_id}/access_tokens ``` does **not** appear to have documented installation-isolated quotas. GitHub’s documentation instead suggests token creation is governed by: - secondary rate limits - abuse detection - authentication throttling - app-level protections GitHub explicitly documents: - excessive token creation may trigger `422` - secondary rate limits apply to authentication-related traffic - high concurrency and burst traffic may be throttled * * * ## Likely Behavior Model The safest interpretation of GitHub’s documentation is: | Area | Behavior | | --- | --- | | Installation API usage | Isolated per installation | | Token generation | Shared app/authentication throttling | | Abuse protection | Centralized | | Secondary rate limits | Shared across the GitHub App | So while installation API quotas scale well across many tenants, token minting itself is likely governed by centralized protections. * * * ## Recommended Architecture ### Cache Tokens Per Installation Reuse installation tokens until close to expiration. Typical strategy: - generate once - store token + expiry - refresh only near expiration - share cached token across workers/requests * * * ### Generate Tokens Lazily Only mint a token when: - no cached token exists - token is close to expiry - token has been revoked * * * ### Avoid Burst Token Creation Do **not**: - create a new token for every request - refresh all tenant tokens simultaneously - spawn large concurrent token-generation floods * * * ### Add Retry/Backoff Logic Handle: - `403` - `429` - secondary rate limits - temporary abuse detection with exponential backoff and jitter. * * * ## Concurrency Considerations Large multi-tenant deployments should: - serialize token refreshes per installation - deduplicate simultaneous refresh attempts - use distributed locking if multiple servers/workers exist Example: If 100 requests arrive simultaneously for the same installation: ### Bad - 100 token creation requests ### Good - 1 refresh request - remaining requests await cached result * * * ## Scaling Expectations GitHub Apps are designed to scale across many organizations safely. The intended scalable pattern is: ``` Many installations ↓ One cached token per installation ↓ Heavy API usage with isolated installation quotas ``` Not: ``` Generate new installation token for every API request ``` * * * ## Practical Recommendation A healthy production pattern is: - cache installation tokens - refresh at ~55 minutes - reuse aggressively - avoid synchronized refresh storms - keep token generation frequency low Under this model, GitHub Apps generally scale well across large multi-tenant deployments. | 1You must be logged in to vote All reactions 1 reply [![@MimiAngpo](https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/214451325?s=60&v=4)](https://github.com/MimiAngpo) Comment options ### Uh oh! [Please reload this page](https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/196652). # {{title}} Quote reply ### [![](https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/145132115?s=64&v=4)\ sahilbhat1](https://github.com/sahilbhat1) [on May 22May 22, 2026](https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/196652\#discussioncomment-17022077) | | | --- | | Installation API usage is isolated per installation, but installation token creation itself is governed by shared authentication throttling, secondary rate limits, and abuse-protection systems rather than a dedicated per-installation quota.
Because of this, while your actual API requests will scale perfectly across multiple organizations, the token generation endpoint (POST /app/installations/{installation\_id}/access\_tokens) can become a bottleneck if you hit it too frequently across a massive multi-tenant architecture.
To safely scale across thousands of organizations, your architecture needs to minimize calls to the generation endpoint. Here is the recommended pattern:
Cache Aggressively: Never generate a new token for every API request. Generate it once, cache it alongside its exact expiration time, and share it across your workers.
Lazy Refreshes: Only request a new token when the current one is within ~5 minutes of expiring.
Concurrency Control: Use distributed locking (e.g., Redis) to handle token expiration. If 100 simultaneous requests arrive for an expired tenant, ensure only one worker attempts the refresh while the remaining 99 await the new cached token.
Avoid Thundering Herds: Do not use a centralized cron job that refreshes all tenant tokens at the exact same second. If you must pre-warm tokens, introduce jitter to spread the API requests out over time.
Handle Rate Limits: Always implement exponential backoff and retry logic for 403 and 429 responses on the token endpoint.

Running multiple app replicas each independently generating tokens for the same installation without a shared cache or distributed lock

A centralized token service — a dedicated internal microservice whose only job is managing the token lifecycle, with a shared distributed cache (Redis/Memcached) backing it
Staggered pre-warming with jitter so tokens don't all expire at the same wall-clock second
Per-installation locking to prevent concurrent refresh storms for the same tenant

[Please reload this page](https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/196652). # {{title}} Quote reply ### [![](https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/100784065?s=64&v=4)\ Ph4ntomic](https://github.com/Ph4ntomic) [on Jun 1Jun 1, 2026](https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/196652\#discussioncomment-17130982) | | | --- | | The important distinction is that “25k requests/minute” should usually not mean “25k installation token creations/minute”.
`POST /app/installations/{installation_id}/access_tokens` is only needed to mint or refresh an installation token. That token then lives for about 1 hour, and the actual API traffic made with that token uses the installation’s own rate limit bucket.
So for example, with 80,000 installations:
```
80,000 installations / 3,600 seconds
≈ 22 token creations per second
≈ 1,333 token creations per minute
```
That is the upper-bound case where every installation needs one fresh token every hour.
In a real multi-tenant system, it is usually lower because many installations are idle at any given moment.
The system becomes risky only if token creation is tied to request volume, for example:
- creating a new installation token for every API request
- refreshing all installation tokens at the same wall-clock time
- having multiple workers refresh the same installation token independently
- creating many different token variants for the same installation because of different `repositories`, `repository_ids`, or `permissions` scopes
A scalable pattern would be:
1. Cache tokens per effective token scope, not just per installation:
- `installation_id`
- requested repositories / repository IDs
- requested permissions
2. Refresh lazily:
- create a token only when no valid cached token exists
- refresh when it is close to expiry, for example 5-10 minutes before `expires_at`
3. Deduplicate refreshes:
- use a per-installation or per-token-scope lock
- if 100 requests arrive for the same expired token, only one worker should call the token endpoint and the others should wait for the cached result
4. Avoid synchronized refresh storms:
- do not pre-refresh every tenant on the hour
- add jitter/spreading if you pre-warm tokens
5. Handle throttling defensively:
- respect `Retry-After` when present
- use exponential backoff with jitter for `403`, `429`, and `422`
- do not retry in tight loops
So yes, GitHub Apps can scale to a large number of installations, but token generation has to be treated as a cached lifecycle operation, not as part of the hot path for every API call.
The per-installation scaling applies clearly to API requests made with installation access tokens. The token creation endpoint itself should be treated more conservatively because it is authenticated with the app JWT and is still subject to secondary/abuse protections. In practice, the safe architecture is “many API calls per cached installation token”, not “one token per API call”.
